ideal_answer_points: Explain the purpose and outcome of each Scrum event
Distinguish between Scrum Master, Product Owner, and Dev Team roles
Describe how Scrum Master serves the team as a servent-leader
Describe how to protect the team from external disruptions
Handle sprint goal commitment vs capacity
Articulate the difference between Scrum and generic Agile
common_mistakes: Treating Scrum Master as a project manager or taskmaster
Skipping or rushing retrospectives
Not empowering the team to self-organize
Confusing velocity with productivity
Allowing the product owner to dictate how work is done

difficulty_expectations.Junior: Understands Scrum events and artifacts, facilitates basic ceremonies
difficulty_expectations.Mid-Level: Coaches team on agile principles, removes impediments proactively
difficulty_expectations.Senior: Drives organizational agile transformation, mentors other Scrum Masters
difficulty_expectations.Staff / Principal: Defines agile strategy across the org, influences enterprise frameworks like SAFe/Less

ideal_answer_points: Choose facilitation technique based on meeting goal and group dynamics
Ensure all voices are heard, not just the loudest
Use visual aids and collaborative tools for remote teams
Keep discussions focused with clear agendas and timeboxes
Handle conflict constructively during ceremonies
common_mistakes: Dominating the conversation instead of facilitating
No agenda or clear goal for the meeting
Letting one person monopolize discussion
Not adapting technique for remote vs in-person
Failing to capture and follow up on action items

difficulty_expectations.Junior: Facilitates standard ceremonies with a template or guide
difficulty_expectations.Mid-Level: Adapts facilitation style to team needs, handles mild conflict
difficulty_expectations.Senior: Designs custom workshops, facilitates cross-team alignment sessions
difficulty_expectations.Staff / Principal: Coaches facilitators org-wide, creates facilitation playbooks

ideal_answer_points: Maintain a visible impediment backlog with ownership and status
Distinguish between team-level and organizational impediments
Use root cause analysis to address systemic issues, not just symptoms
Escalate appropriately when impediments are beyond team control
Track resolution time and patterns to prevent recurring blockers
common_mistakes: Solving problems for the team instead of coaching them to solve it
Ignoring organizational impediments because they are hard
No follow-up or tracking on raised impediments
Treating symptoms rather than root causes
Not leveraging management support for escalations

difficulty_expectations.Junior: Identifies and logs impediments raised in standups
difficulty_expectations.Mid-Level: Proactively identifies blockers, resolves most within the team
difficulty_expectations.Senior: Tackles organizational impediments, builds escalation frameworks
difficulty_expectations.Staff / Principal: Drives systemic change to eliminate classes of impediments org-wide

ideal_answer_points: Explain servant leadership as prioritizing team needs over personal authority
Demonstrate coaching vs directing based on team maturity
Build psychological safety so team members speak up without fear
Empower the team to self-organize and make decisions
Adapt leadership style based on context and individual needs
common_mistakes: Being passive and calling it 'servant leadership'
Not holding the team accountable to their own commitments
Avoiding difficult conversations to maintain harmony
Taking over tasks instead of coaching the team through them
Confusing consensus with collaboration

difficulty_expectations.Junior: Understands the concept, supports team members when asked
difficulty_expectations.Mid-Level: Actively coaches team members, builds trust through consistency
difficulty_expectations.Senior: Models servant leadership for the org, mentors new Scrum Masters
difficulty_expectations.Staff / Principal: Shapes leadership culture, influences exec leadership toward servant-leader principles

ideal_answer_points: Use velocity for forecasting, never as a performance measure
Track cycle time and lead time to identify process bottlenecks
Balance quantitative metrics with qualitative health indicators
Use metrics to drive conversations, not to punish the team
Avoid vanity metrics; focus on outcomes over output
common_mistakes: Using velocity to compare teams
Inflating story points to appear more productive
Ignoring qualitative metrics like team morale
Over-indexing on a single metric
Not explaining metrics in context to stakeholders

difficulty_expectations.Junior: Tracks velocity and burndown, reports to the team
difficulty_expectations.Mid-Level: Analyzes trends, uses metrics to guide retrospective topics
difficulty_expectations.Senior: Designs metric dashboards, coaches teams and stakeholders on interpretation
difficulty_expectations.Staff / Principal: Defines org-wide agile metrics strategy, aligns metrics with business outcomes

ideal answer points: Use Sprint Review to create transparency and gather genuine feedback
Shield the team from disruptive stakeholder requests mid-sprint
Maintain regular communication cadence with key stakeholders
Help Product Owner manage stakeholder priorities effectively
Build trust by delivering consistently and communicating honestly
common mistakes: Allowing stakeholders to bypass Product Owner and assign work directly
No transparency into team progress until end of sprint
Over-promising to stakeholders to avoid conflict
Not involving stakeholders early enough for feedback
Treating stakeholder management as solely the PO's job

difficulty_expectations.Junior: Invites stakeholders to Sprint Review, shares updates as requested
difficulty_expectations.Mid-Level: Proactively manages expectations, coaches PO on stakeholder prioritization
difficulty_expectations.Senior: Builds strategic relationships with senior stakeholders, aligns multiple teams
difficulty_expectations.Staff / Principal: Shares org-wide stakeholder engagement model, advises executives on agile governance

ideal_answer_points: Recognize and support the team through forming-storming-norming-performing stages
Create working agreements collaboratively and revisit them regularly
Foster self-organization by giving the team ownership of how they work
Address interpersonal conflict early before it escalates
Build cross-functional capability so the team can deliver end-to-end
common_mistakes: Ignoring team conflict hoping it resolves itself
Imposing working agreements top-down
Not celebrating successes or recognizing individual contributions
Allowing silos within the team
Expecting a new team to perform like a mature team immediately

difficulty_expectations.Junior: Observes team dynamics, flags issues to senior colleagues
difficulty_expectations.Mid-Level: Actively nurtures team health, facilitates conflict resolution
difficulty_expectations.Senior: Builds high-performing teams from scratch, coaches through major transitions
difficulty_expectations.Staff / Principal: Designs team topologies and org structures that optimize for flow and autonomy

ideal_answer_points: Use retrospectives as the primary driver of continuous improvement
Frame improvements as experiments with clear success criteria
Track action items from retros and hold the team accountable
Create short feedback loops to validate improvements quickly
Apply lean thinking to eliminate waste in processes
common_mistakes: Running retrospectives but never acting on outcomes
Trying to change too many things at once
No measurement of whether improvements actually helped
Only focusing on process, ignoring technical practices
Treating improvement as a one-time activity rather than ongoing

difficulty_expectations.Junior: Participates in retros, follows through on assigned action items
difficulty_expectations.Mid-Level: Facilitates effective retros, tracks improvement experiments
difficulty_expectations.Senior: Creates a culture of continuous improvement across teams
difficulty_expectations.Staff / Principal: Builds org-wide learning systems, drives improvement at the enterprise level
